learn.pageTitle: Why Riichi Mahjong Scoring Is Hard to Learn
learn.pageDescription: The three reasons I, the author, struggled to learn riichi mahjong scoring, and how they shaped the way this app is built.
learn.lead1:
Riichi mahjong scoring is hard.
Here, “being able to score” means being able to recite the correct score smoothly whenever you [[hora|win]] a hand at a real table.
learn.lead2:
It took me a very long time to get there myself.
Looking back, I think these were the reasons I could not learn scoring quickly.
learn.reason1Summary: It was so complex that I could not even tell what I did not understand
learn.reason2Summary: I did not get enough repetition
learn.reason3Summary: I could not cope with the subtleties of playing at a real table
learn.reason1Title: It was so complex that I could not even tell what I did not understand
learn.reason1Body1:
First, if you try to calculate scores below [[mangan|mangan]] without understanding fu, it naturally makes no sense.
For example, someone once told me, “In mahjong the score just doubles with every han, so even a grade-schooler can work it out.”
In reality, though, scores often do not simply double, as in 1000, 2000, 3900 or 2000, 3900, 7700.
learn.reason1Note: * There is a reason scores grow this irregularly; it is explained in another lesson.
learn.reason1Body2:
Also, whether a score involves fu or is mangan and above, you need to understand yaku and count han.
Scoring is built from several skills combined like this, so there is a lot to learn in the first place, and I did not know what to learn first.
learn.reason2Title: I did not get enough repetition
learn.reason2Body1:
At first, I read a little of an introductory mahjong book and tried to learn scoring through beginner lessons at mahjong parlors and at mahjong classes.
Classroom-style lessons like these have the advantage that experts teach you correct knowledge, but they are often passive and centered on listening.
I had few chances to actually work through problems myself, so in my case it did not stick.
learn.reason2Body2:
People who can visit parlors and classes often can probably get enough practice, but I think many people are too busy to make the time.
Even just securing chances to gain experience at a real table costs a great deal.
I think learning scoring naturally just by playing lots of games is unrealistic.
learn.reason3Title: I could not cope with the subtleties of playing at a real table
learn.reason3Body1:
If you are trying to learn scoring, you probably want to play at a physical mahjong table rather than online.
After all, online mahjong calculates the score for you.
learn.reason3Body2:
Even so, after using other apps heavily until I could score instantly, I still could not score that quickly at a real table.
Looking back, I think it was because real games differ in many ways from the scoring problems an app gives you: from your starting hand you have to anticipate, to some extent, which yaku you will build, and you have to hand over point sticks.
learn.afterword: This app is built to remove these three stumbling blocks one by one. How it does so is described in “<link></link>”.
